text: This library is a set of React components that can be used to build resizable layouts like the one below: main App.tsx Hide panel There are three kinds of layouts: flex layouts of panels in a row or column, grids of cells that resize in two dimensions, and workspaces of tabsets that users can rearrange by dragging tabs. Check out the support page if you have questions. Installation Begin by installing the library from NPM: TypeScript definitions are included within the published dist folder. Support Here are some ways to support this project: Become a GitHub sponsor Buy me a coffee
title: Getting started with react-resizable-panels

headings.title: Why do I see an "invalid panel layout" error?
headings.text: Why do I see an "invalid panel layout" error? This error means that a Group layout (or the sum total of Panel default sizes) does not add up to 100%. If the layout you've specified does add up to 100, the most likely remaining cause is that you've specified sizes as pixels rather than percentages as per this note from the Panel docs: Numeric values are assumed to be pixels. Strings without explicit units are assumed to be percentages (0%..100%).

headings.title: Why is a vertical group not visible?
headings.text: Why is a vertical group not visible? By default, Group elements specify a default style height:100%. However according to the w3 spec: The percentage is calculated with respect to the height of the generated box's containing block. If the height of the containing block is not specified explicitly (i.e., it depends on content height), and this element is not absolutely positioned, the value computes to "auto". Put another way, fixing this requires setting an explicit height either on the Group itself or on its parent HTMLElement. Note that because the default height is an inline style, it can only be overridden by another inline style or an !important CSS rule.

headings.title: ReferenceError: localStorage is not defined
headings.text: ReferenceError: localStorage is not defined The useDefaultLayout hook saves layouts to localStorage by default. This does not work for server-rendered applications though, since localStorage is only defined on the client. Refer to the server rendering or server components docs for examples of how to save layouts on the server.

headings.title: How can I conditionally render a Panel based on screen size?
headings.text: How can I conditionally render a Panel based on screen size? The recommended way is to use the ResizeObserver API, either through a hook like useResizeObserver or a component like react-virtualized-auto-sizer. Putting the defaultSize on the conditional Panel is the easiest way to avoid invalid layout constraints in this type of scenario.

text: Collapsible panels with a collapsedSize can be used to build an accordion, like the sections in VS Code's explorer. Each section collapses down to the height of its header, so the header stays visible and can be clicked to expand it again. Each header uses the useParentPanel hook to collapse or expand the panel it's rendered in; expanding a section takes space from the nearest open sections. The demo below also keeps at least one section open, and uses each panel's onResize callback to keep its header in sync when sections are resized by dragging. Click a header below to collapse or expand its section, or drag between sections to resize them.
title: Accordion

text: As with panels, a grid's columns and rows can be configured to collapse when they're resized below their minimum size. This works well for things like dashboards, where a sidebar can collapse down to just its icons and secondary content can be hidden entirely. Try dragging the gridlines below. The row gridline only spans the second column because the sidebar spans both rows.
title: Collapsible cells

text: Panels can be configured to collapse when they're resized below their minimum size. This enables building UIs like VS Code's side panel. Try dragging the separator to collapse the side panel. Panels are made collapsible using the collapsible and minSize properties. Although it isn't required, it's recommended that you also render a Separator for panels that can be collapsed fully. This separator gives users something to click to re-open a panel after it's been collapsed. The collapsedSize property can also be provided to prevent a panel from disappearing fully when collapsed. Collapsible panels can also be collapsed by default by setting their defaultSize to 0 (pixels or percent). By default, panels will collapse (or expand) when resized beyond the midpoint of their collapsed and minimum sizes. (For example, a panel with a collapsed size of 0 and a minimum size of 20% will collapse when resized below 10%.) The collapsedThreshold prop can be used to customize this behavior.
title: Collapsible panels

text: Panels can be conditionally rendered. Conditional panels should also specify ids to help match previous, saved layouts. It is recommended to use usePanelCallbackRef rather than usePanelRef when attaching a ref to a conditionally-rendered panel. See issue #717 for more information.
title: Conditional panels

text: className and style props can be used to customize styles, but there are a few limitations to remember: Certain style properties cannot be overridden; (refer to component documentation for a list of specific styles) Panel styles are applied to a nested HTMLDivElement to prevent interfering with the Flex layout When styling a Separator, use the data-separator attribute rather than :hover or :active pseudo-classes. This attribute is updated when the pointer is near enough to a separator element to be interactive, even if it is not directly on top of the element. An example using Tailwind CSS might look something like this. If you want to differentiate between keyboard-initiated focus and pointer-initiated focus, you can use the :focus and :focus-visible CSS pseudo-classes instead.
title: Styling

text: Panel and Separator components can be disabled to disable or limit resize behavior. Below are a few examples of how this can be used to implement different types of UIs. In groups with only two panels, disabling a separator is sufficient to completely prevent resizing. The same applies to disabling one or both panels when there is no explicit separator element. Note this is functionally the same as disabling the entire Group component. In groups with three or more panels, disabling a separator does not completely prevent a panel from being resized. In the example below, resizing the center panel can indirectly cause the left panel to be resized as well. Disabling a panel prevents it from being resized, though its separator can still be used to resize other panels. When there is no separator, a disabled panel's edges can also be used to resize other panels. You can also disable both a panel and its separator to completely prevent them from being resized or interacted with in any way. Note that a disabled Panel can still be resized using the imperative API.
title: Disabled panels

text: You can also render non-interactive elements inside of a group if you need fixed-size content. Non-interactive elements can also be rendered between panels. As with other types of groups, separators are optional (but recommended).
title: Fixed size panels

text: The Grid component arranges resizable Cells in two dimensions. Columns are resized horizontally and rows are resized vertically. Dragging the point where a column boundary meets a row boundary resizes both at once. A50% × 50% B50% × 50% C50% × 50% D50% × 50% Cells can span multiple columns (columnSpan) and/or rows (rowSpan). A boundary cannot be resized alongside of a cell that spans across it, although it can still be resized elsewhere. header100% × 33% sidebar33% × 67% A33% × 33% B33% × 33% footer67% × 33%

text: Columns and rows support the same size constraints as panels, although they are declared on the grid rather than on individual cells because cells can span multiple rows or columns. left25% × 100% top75% × 25% bottom75% × 75% As with panels, sizes can be specified using the following CSS units: Pixels Percentages Font sizes (em, rem) Viewport sizes (vh, vw)

text: Grids can be configured to save and restore layouts (the sizes of their columns and rows) between page visits with the useDefaultGridLayout hook. Resize the grid below and then reload the page to see an example. A50% × 50% B50% × 50% C50% × 50% D50% × 50% A saved layout is ignored for an axis if its track ids don't match the Grid's (e.g. after a column has been added or removed). The hook works the same way as useDefaultLayout does for groups, so the same guidance applies to server rendering (e.g. saving layouts in a cookie instead of localStorage).

text: Like Separators within a Group, Gridlines are optional but recommended because they make the grid accessible to keyboard users. A <Gridline type="column" /> resizes the columns on either side of it and spans all rows A <Gridline type="row" /> resizes the rows on either side of it and spans all columns Where they intersect, dragging resizes both. A33% × 50% B33% × 50% C33% × 50% D33% × 50% E33% × 50% F33% × 50% By default, gridlines span to fill the available width/height. If a grid contains cells that span multiple rows or columns though, you may need to render multiple gridlines. A33% × 50% B33% × 50% C33% × 100% D33% × 50% E33% × 50% Once a boundary contains a gridline, it can only be resized using gridlines; the parts of the boundary that aren't alongside of a gridline can't be dragged.
title: Gridlines

text: Resizing a group typically affects the size of panels within the group. The groupResizeBehavior prop can be used to override this behavior and freeze specific panels (in terms of their pixel sizes) while the group is resized. For an example of this, resize the browser window while keeping an eye on the left panel below. Minor pixel changes in the panel above are due to precision/rounding. Groups are required to contain at least one panel without groupResizeBehavior="preserve-pixel-size".
title: Group resize behavior

text: Panels can be configured with minimum/maximum allowed sizes. Size can be specified using the following CSS units: Pixels Percentages Font sizes (em, rem) Viewport sizes (vh, vw) For example, the left panel below only allows itself to be resized between 100-200 pixels. As another example, this panel group will not allow any individual panel to be smaller than 10% of the group's width. When specifying sizes, remember: Numbers are evaluated as pixels. Strings are evaluated as percentages (0..100%) unless otherwise specified. You can always include the unit, even for pixels (e.g. minSize="100px") or percentages (e.g. minSize="10%")
title: Min/max sizes

text: Panel groups can be nested. In this configuration, multiple groups can be resized at the same time by clicking near panel intersections. For example, the email client below nests a vertical group (the message list and reading pane) inside of a horizontal one. Try dragging the point where all three panels meet. If your nested panels form a grid (e.g. each row has the same columns), consider using the Grid component instead.
title: Nested groups

To enable Panels to have overflowing visual styles (like shadows or outlines) you need to change the group overflow style to "visible": If you change the overflow style, it is recommended that you also specify an explicit width/height on the group. For example, this group of panels demonstrates a drop-shadow style. And this group demonstrates a focus outline style. The panel sets a higher z-index on focus-within to avoid clipping issues. Styles that affect the outer panel element (e.g. shadows, outlines) work without any customizations. Things like tooltips or popovers that are rendered inside of the panel will be clipped by the overflow:auto style. Because of this it's recommended to use portals for these. However you can override the default style as shown below. All of the above styles also apply to the separator component. You could also use the data-separator='focus' selector.

text: Dragging a resize separator causes panels to re-render with updated sizes. In most cases, this is what you want, but if re-rendering the contents of a panel is too slow, the resizePreviewMode prop can be used to defer the re-render until the resize is finished. In place of a panel update, an overlay separator will be rendered instead. In the group below, the panels (and their sizes) only update once the separator is released. By default, this overlay separator is just a partially transparent copy of the separator element being dragged. The SeparatorOverlay component allows users to customize the overlay. Resize preview mode works even for groups with implicit separators. The data-separator-overlay attribute can be used to differentiate between a separator that's being actively dragged and one that's being moved as a result of min/max size constraints.
title: Panel resize behavior

text: The simplest resizable panel configuration is two panels within a group. Panel groups use a flexbox layout with a default orientation of horizontal but the orientation prop can be used to specify a vertical layout. Vertical groups may benefit from an explicit height or min-height (read more). Panels can be resized by clicking on their borders but explicit separators can be rendered to improve UX. Separators provide another benefit: double-clicking on one resets a panel to its default size. Separators improve keyboard accessibility by providing a tab-focusable window splitter element.
title: The basics

text: A Workspace arranges tabsets, like an IDE's editor groups. Users can rearrange them by dragging tabs between tabsets, within a tabset's list of tabs, or onto the edge of a tabset to split it. Tabsets can also be resized and maximized. Reset layout Tab content is never remounted when a tab is moved, so it keeps its state. Try incrementing the counter above and then dragging its tab somewhere else. Workspaces are uncontrolled. Their arrangement of tabsets and tabs is described by a serializable model, which can be observed using the onModelChanged callback. Splits lay out their children side by side or stacked, and tabsets show one tab at a time. Sizes are percentages of the parent split; siblings without a size share the remaining space. Initial sizes can also be strings with units (e.g. "250px"), but they're converted to percentages when the user resizes the split, and they scale with the workspace when it's resized. This is the model for the workspace above: The tabsetMinWidth and tabsetMinHeight props above set a minimum size for the content of every tabset (not including its tabs); a tabset can override them with the minWidth and minHeight fields of its model node. Tabsets can also have maximum sizes (see limiting tabset sizes). Tabs can also be opened, selected, closed, and rearranged by the application (see managing tabs and managing tabsets). Like the rest of the library, workspaces are unstyled; see custom tabsets and styling for how to render and style tabsets. The tabsets above are resized by dragging the boundary between them; see separators and accessibility for how to render visible separators, and how workspaces can be used with the keyboard.
title: The basics

headings.title: Renaming tabs
headings.text: Renaming tabs A tab can show an input in place of its title, e.g. after it's double-clicked or F2 is pressed, and save the new title with the updateTab method of the imperative API. Pressing Enter or moving focus away saves the title, and Escape cancels. Keys typed in the input don't move focus between tabs or close the tab.

headings.title: Toolbars that run out of room
headings.text: Toolbars that run out of room A tabset's tab list fills the space its tabs and toolbar don't use, so a toolbar can't tell how much room it has by measuring itself. The useTabListFreeSpace hook returns the space in the tab list that its tabs don't use (negative once they overflow). A toolbar can use that space in addition to its own, e.g. to move items into a "…" menu once they no longer fit: Place items only when the free space changes. Each value is measured with the toolbar as it's shown at the time, so it pairs with the toolbar's current size. Placing items again after the toolbar changes (but before the free space is measured again) counts the change twice, and the toolbar can keep switching between two layouts. Resize the tabsets below (or add tabs) to see their toolbars' items move into and out of their menus. Reset layout The hook (like the --tab-list-free-space custom property on the tab list) is updated before the browser paints, so moved items are never shown in the wrong place. To read it outside of a tabset (e.g. a toolbar rendered elsewhere and portaled into the tabset), use the getTabListFreeSpace and subscribeToTabListFreeSpace methods of the imperative API; listeners are called synchronously, before the browser paints.

headings.title: Tabs that don't fit
headings.text: Tabs that don't fit When a tabset has more tabs than fit, its tab list scrolls. The useTabListOverflow hook returns which of its tabs are out of view (and which are only partly visible), e.g. for a menu that lists them: A selected tab is scrolled into view, however it's selected (e.g. from the menu, or with the selectTab method). In the workspace below, scroll the tab list (or make the tabset narrower) and select tabs from the menu. Reset layout To read which tabs are out of view outside of a tabset, use the getTabListOverflow and subscribeToTabListOverflow methods of the imperative API. Like the rest of the library, tabsets are unstyled; see styling.

text: By default, each tabset shows a list of tabs (with close buttons) above its content. The tabPlacement prop moves the list to another side, and these props customize what a tabset contains: renderTab renders each tab. renderTabsetToolbar renders content after the tabs (e.g. buttons to add a tab or maximize the tabset). renderEmptyTabset renders content in tabsets without tabs. renderTab receives the props that make an element a tab (its role and ARIA attributes, keyboard and pointer handling, data attributes, and a ref); spread them onto the element it returns. The TabCloseButton component closes the tab it's rendered within. Buttons, form controls (e.g. input) the labels of form controls, editable content, and elements with a button or form control role (e.g. role="checkbox") or a data-tab-ignore attribute within a tab don't select or drag it. Props can be overridden or wrapped. For example, to confirm before closing a tab with unsaved changes (whether by its close button or the Delete or Backspace key):
title: Custom tabsets

headings.text: Adding tabs from a tabset Components within a tabset (e.g. a button rendered by renderTabsetToolbar) can add tabs to that tabset with the useParentTabset hook:

headings.title: Updating and closing tabs
headings.text: Updating and closing tabs The updateTab method changes a tab's title, data, or flags, and closeTab closes it. Within a tab's content, the useParentTab hook returns the tab, so content can update or close its own tab: A tab's data is replaced rather than merged when it is updated. To confirm before the user closes a tab (e.g. one with unsaved changes), see custom tabsets. Changes made with the imperative API are reported by onModelChanged (with isUserInteraction set to false), so they're saved like any other change. Users can also drag new tabs in from outside of the workspace, and the tab that's selected when the selected tab is closed can be customized. To keep, move, resize, collapse, maximize, or float whole tabsets, see managing tabsets.

text: Tabs are usually opened in response to something outside of the workspace (e.g. a file being selected in a tree). The imperative API's addTab method adds a tab to the active tabset (the one the user most recently interacted with) and selects it: If a tab with the same id is already open (anywhere in the workspace), it's selected instead, and addTab returns false. Options can add the tab to a specific tabset (tabsetId) or position (index), or add it without selecting it (select: false). The target option adds the tab anywhere a tab can be dropped, including in a new tabset beside another tabset or along an edge of the workspace (the same targets moveTab accepts), and size sets the new tabset's share of its split: Open Notes Open About Add content using the buttons above
title: Managing tabs

headings.title: Making copies
headings.text: Making copies A copy needs an id that isn't used by any other tab or tabset in the workspace. Copies with ids that are already in use are rejected (with a warning during development), and the tab is moved instead, as it is when copyTab returns null. Both props are called with where the copy will be dropped, so some targets can move tabs rather than copy them. copyTabset returns the whole copy, including its tabs; its copyTab argument copies a tab with the copyTab prop (or, without it, as a shallow copy with a new id). The copy's selected tab is the copy of the dragged tabset's selected tab. Copies are reported to onModelChanged with the "copy" reason, and the disableDrop prop is told whether a copy would be dropped (isCopy), e.g. to only allow copies in some tabsets (see restrictions).

headings.title: Showing that a drag copies
headings.text: Showing that a drag copies The renderDragPreview and renderTabsetDragPreview props are told whether dropping would add a copy (isCopy): The drag preview and the drop indicator also have a data-drag-copy attribute then, for styling.

headings.title: Between workspaces
headings.text: Between workspaces Tabs dragged between workspaces with the same drag group are copied by the workspace they're dropped into, so it needs the copyTab prop (the workspace they're dragged from doesn't change). In other copies of your app, the copy is made from the tab data that was sent there. These drags use the browser's drag and drop, which shows the system's copy cursor while the copy key is held over a workspace that would copy.

text: Dragging a tab moves it. With the copyTab prop, users can drop a copy instead (e.g. a second chart with the same settings) by holding the copy key while dragging. The copyTabset prop does the same for tabsets (dragged by their headers): Reset layout The copy key is ⌥ on macOS and ctrl on other platforms.
title: Copying tabs

headings.title: Starting a drag
headings.text: Starting a drag Call startExternalDrag from an element's pointerdown handler with the tab to add. The tab is dragged like the workspace's own tabs are, and added where it's dropped: The drag starts once the pointer moves, so clicking the element still works (e.g. to add the tab with addTab; see managing tabs), and the click that follows a drag is suppressed. Pressing Escape cancels the drag. startExternalDrag returns a promise that resolves with where the tab was dropped ({ target }), or null if it wasn't (e.g. it was dropped outside of the workspace, or the drag was canceled). The element that follows the pointer shows what the Workspace's renderDragPreview prop renders for the tab, unless a preview is passed. Set touch-action: none on the element, so that touch input drags it rather than scrolling the page. The element must be in the same document as the workspace; tabs dragged this way can't be dropped into a workspace in another window (see multiple windows).

headings.title: Accepting the browser's drag and drop
headings.text: Accepting the browser's drag and drop Browsers only let a drag's data be read when it's dropped, so the acceptExternalDrop prop has two parts: the data types that decide where the drop indicator is shown while the drag is over the workspace, and a createTab function that reads the data and creates the tab when it's dropped: createTab can return null to reject the drop. Files dragged from the operating system have the "Files" type: Elements within tabs' content that accept a drag themselves (by canceling its dragover event) take precedence over the workspace. Drags of the workspace's own tabs (see the dragGroup prop) are never passed to createTab.

headings.title: Restrictions
headings.text: Restrictions Tabs dragged in either way are checked by the disableDrop prop with the "new" source, and can't be dropped into a workspace that already has a tab (or tabset) with the same id, so give each new tab a unique id. Neither works while the workspace is disabled. Unlike the rest of the imperative API, startExternalDrag is restricted by these, since the user decides where the tab goes (see restrictions). A drag's data can't be read until it's dropped, so for drags that use the browser's drag and drop, disableDrop is only called when it's dropped (with the tab createTab returned); the drop indicator may be shown over a target that ends up rejecting it. New tabs are reported to onModelChanged with the "add" reason (and isUserInteraction set to true).

text: Users can drag new tabs in from outside of the workspace (e.g. from a library of widgets), and drop them anywhere a tab could be dropped: into a tabset, beside one, or at an edge of the workspace. There are two ways to do this: The startExternalDrag method of the imperative API starts a drag that works like dragging one of the workspace's own tabs, including with touch input. The acceptExternalDrop prop accepts drags that use the browser's drag and drop, e.g. elements with the draggable attribute, files, or drags from another application. Drag the widgets below into the workspace. "Counter" and "Notes" use startExternalDrag, and "About" uses the browser's drag and drop. headings.title: Selecting a tab after one is closed
headings.text: Selecting a tab after one is closed When the selected tab is closed (or dragged to another tabset), the tab after it is selected by default. With the tabRemovalSelectionBehavior prop set to "recent", the tab that was selected before it is selected instead, like in an IDE: In the workspace below, select a few tabs and then close the selected one. About Counter Notes Nested panels Drag a tab onto another tab list to move it there. Drag a tab onto the edge of a tabset to split it, or onto its center to add the tab to it. Use the arrow keys to move between tabs, Enter to select one, and Delete to close one. Clicked 0 times Increment Reset layout Each tabset's recently selected tabs are saved in the model (as recentTabIds ), so they're restored with the rest of the model. If none of the remaining tabs has been selected, the tab after the closed one is selected.

text: Each tabset's selected tab is saved in the model as its selectedId . The imperative selectTab method selects a tab by id (in whichever tabset contains it):
title: Selecting tabs

headings.title: Empty tabsets
headings.text: Empty tabsets By default, a tabset is removed when its last tab is closed or dragged away. A tabset with the keepWhenEmpty flag stays instead (e.g. an editor area that should remain as a drop target), showing the Workspace's renderEmptyTabset content, until it's closed with the closeTabset method or the useParentTabset hook's close function. The example hides its close button in the only tabset in the workspace, since closing it would just close its tabs: In the workspace below, the tabset on the right has the keepWhenEmpty flag. Close its tabs (or drag them into the tabset on the left) and it stays, as a place to drop them again. Each tabset's close button (×) removes it, along with any tabs it still has. Reset layout Closing a tabset also closes any tabs it contains. Like the rest of the imperative API, it isn't restricted by tabs' disableClose flags.

headings.title: Moving tabsets
headings.text: Moving tabsets Users can drag a whole tabset by the empty space in its header (e.g. after its last tab). Dropping it onto the edge of another tabset moves it there; dropping it onto the center of another tabset (or into its list of tabs) moves its tabs into that tabset instead. A TabsetDragHandle (or any element with a data-tabset-drag-handle attribute) within a tabset's header replaces its empty space: once a header has a handle, only the handle drags the tabset. The handle has a data-disabled attribute while the tabset can't be dragged (e.g. to hide or dim it). Reset layout Tabsets with the keepWhenEmpty flag can be moved, but their tabs can't be dropped into another tabset with them (which would leave the tabset behind, empty). Tabsets can't be dragged when they (or any of their tabs) have the disableDrag flag (see restrictions), when they're the only tabset, or while a tabset is maximized. The moveTabset method moves a tabset from outside of the workspace (e.g. a "Move to bottom" menu item); it accepts the same targets as moveTab.

headings.title: Dropping at the edges of the workspace
headings.text: Dropping at the edges of the workspace Dropping a tab (or tabset) at the very edge of the workspace puts it beside all of the other tabsets, filling the workspace's height (or width), like a sidebar or a bottom panel in an IDE. It takes an equal share of the space, which the other tabsets beside it give up proportionally. Each edge accepts drops within a few pixels of the edges of the workspace's tabsets (further in, the edges of the tabsets themselves accept them), and anywhere within the padding of the workspace's root element. Tabset headers aren't part of the edge, so that drops into their tab lists stay precise; an edge lined with tab lists (e.g. the top of the workspace, by default) only accepts drops within the root element's padding, so add padding there to enable it. These targets have an edge rather than a tabsetId (e.g. { edge: "right" }), and can be turned off with disableDrop={({ target }) => "edge" in target}. The drop indicator has a data-edge attribute (rather than data-region) while it shows one.

text: Tabsets are created and removed as tabs are opened, closed, and dragged (see managing tabs), but they can also be kept when empty and moved as a whole. They can also be limited in size, collapsed, and maximized, and floated above the layout.
title: Managing tabsets

headings.title: Moving and resizing floating tabsets
headings.text: Moving and resizing floating tabsets Users move a floating tabset by dragging its header (the empty space after its tabs, or its TabsetDragHandle), resize it by dragging its edges, and bring it to the front by pressing it. Its tabs can be dragged into the layout and other tabs can be dropped into it; once its last tab is dragged away, it's removed (unless it has the keepWhenEmpty flag). Floating tabsets stay within the workspace: their headers are kept within the layout (so they can always be dragged back), and the rest of them is clipped to it.

headings.title: Collapsing floating tabsets
headings.text: Collapsing floating tabsets Floating tabsets can always be collapsed to just their headers (they don't need the collapsible flag), with the collapseTabset method (or the collapse function of the useParentTabset hook). A collapsed floating tabset keeps its width and height to expand to; until then, it can only be resized along its header. Clicking one of its tabs (or the empty space in its header) expands it.

headings.title: Floating and docking tabsets
headings.text: Floating and docking tabsets The floatTab and floatTabset methods (and the float functions of the useParentTab and useParentTabset hooks) move a tab or tabset into a new floating tabset; moving a floating tabset beside the others (e.g. with moveTabset) docks it. The only tabset in a workspace fills it, so it can't float, which is why the button below renders nothing for it: In the workspace below, drag the notepad by its header, or use the buttons in each tabset's toolbar to float, collapse, and dock it. Notes Reset layout Floating tabsets can't be split or maximized: tabs dropped anywhere on one are added to it, and they're shown above a maximized tabset. Their elements have data-floating-tabset attributes (and data-tabset-collapsed attributes while collapsed; their tabsets have data-tabset-floating attributes), and the floatingTabset and floatingResizeHandle keys of the classNames prop style them. Changes made with the imperative API are reported by onModelChanged (with isUserInteraction set to false), so they're saved like any other change.

text: A tabset can float above the layout, e.g. a notepad that can be moved out of the way of the content beneath it. Floating tabsets are listed in the model's floating field, in stacking order (the last one is on top), with their positions and sizes in pixels. Positions are relative to the top left corner of the layout, even in right-to-left layouts:
title: Floating tabsets

headings.title: Limiting tabset sizes
headings.text: Limiting tabset sizes The maxWidth and maxHeight fields of a tabset limit how large it can be resized, e.g. a sidebar that can only grow so wide. Like minWidth and minHeight, they apply to the tabset's content area (not including its tabs), and must use absolute units (e.g. "300px" or "20rem"): The sidebar below can be resized between 150 and 300 pixels wide, but its tab can't be dragged or closed. Reset layout A split always fills its space, so a maximum only applies if something else can take up the rest of it, e.g. another tabset in the same split without a maximum. Maximums are ignored (with a warning in development) if every tabset in a split has one, or if the tabset fills the workspace.

headings.title: Collapsing tabsets
headings.text: Collapsing tabsets A tabset with the collapsible flag can be collapsed to just its header (e.g. a bottom panel or a sidebar). Like a collapsible Panel, it collapses when a separator is dragged past its minimum size, and expands when the separator is dragged back. Clicking one of its tabs (or the empty space in its header) also expands it, as does dropping a tab into it from another tabset. Its collapsed flag is part of the model, and its size is the size it expands to: Tabsets can also be collapsed and expanded with the collapseTabset and expandTabset methods, or from within a tabset with the useParentTabset hook. The TabsetCollapseButton component does this from a tabset's toolbar, with the ARIA attributes a toggle needs (aria-expanded and aria-controls); its children, className, style, and title can be functions of the tabset's state: In the workspace below, the bottom tabset starts collapsed and the sidebar can be collapsed (with the − button in its toolbar, or by dragging the space beside it). While collapsed, a tabset's header runs along its split, so the sidebar collapses to a vertical strip. Reset layout The only tabset in a workspace can't be collapsed, and neither can a tabset whose siblings are all collapsed (something has to fill the space). Collapsing a tabset doesn't unmount its content. Floating tabsets can always be collapsed, without the collapsible flag (see collapsing floating tabsets).

headings.title: Maximizing tabsets
headings.text: Maximizing tabsets A maximized tabset covers the rest of the workspace until it's restored. The maximizeTabset and restoreTabset methods do this from outside of the workspace, and the useParentTabset hook from within a tabset. The TabsetMaximizeButton component does this from a tabset's toolbar (with aria-pressed): Which tabset is maximized is part of the model, so it's saved and restored with the rest of the model. While a tabset is maximized, tabs can only be dragged within it (or within floating tabsets, which are shown above it).

text: Tabsets are resized by dragging the separators between them (see separators), within their minimum sizes (see the basics). They can also have maximum sizes, be collapsed to just their headers, and be maximized to cover the rest of the workspace.
title: Sizing tabsets

headings.title: Drag groups
headings.text: Drag groups Workspaces with the same dragGroup prop can drag tabs (and tabsets) to each other. A tab dropped into another workspace keeps the same id and data and both workspaces report the change to onModelChanged with the reason "transfer". Tab ids must be unique within the group. A tab can't be dropped into a workspace that already has a tab with its id. The disableDrop function will receive source: "external" for tabs dragged from other workspaces. Pointer events don't span window, so mouse drags use native HTML drag and drop when dragGroup is set. (Touch and pen drags still use pointer events and stay within their window.)

headings.title: Tab content in other windows
headings.text: Tab content in other windows Unlike tabs moved within a workspace, a tab that's dropped into another workspace (or opened in a popout window) will be rendered inside of the new Workspace. State that should survive the move belongs in the tab's data then rather than component state. The workspace a tab is dropped into renders it with its own renderTab and renderTabContent props, so workspaces in a group should be able to render each other's tabs.

text: Tabs (and tabsets) don't have to stay in the window they started in. A Workspace can be rendered into a popout window opened by your app and tabs can be dragged between workspaces in different windows. This functionality is enabled using the dragGroup prop.
title: Multiple windows

text: Workspaces in other copies of your app from the same origin (e.g. your app loaded in another browser window or tab) are part of the same drag group. A tab dropped into another copy will be handed off using a structured clone algorithm (like postMessage). Each copy renders its Workspace with the same dragGroup: Each frame below loads its own copy of a small app with a workspace, so tabs dragged between them are sent between copies. localhost:3200/embed/app?copy=a localhost:3200/embed/app?copy=b Tab data must be cloneable (e.g. no functions); tabs whose data can't be cloned can only be dragged within their copy of your app. Copies loaded at different times may be running different versions of your app, so the other copy may get tab data it doesn't recognize. Set the disableDragBetweenApps prop to keep a workspace's drags within its copy of your app. Workspaces in popout windows rendered by that copy are still part of the group.
title: Copies of your app

headings.title: Dragging between popout windows
headings.text: Dragging between popout windows Workspaces with the same dragGroup prop can drag tabs (and tabsets) to each other, e.g. from a popout window back into the main window, or from one popout to another (see drag groups for how tabs move between workspaces).

headings.title: Rendering into popout windows
headings.text: Rendering into popout windows To open popout windows without usePopoutWindows, elements in a popout window should be created by that window's own document (e.g. the container the Workspace is rendered into), so that they belong to that window. The Workspace and its tabsets read the globals they need (e.g. ResizeObserver) from the window their elements are in.

text: The usePopoutWindows hook opens tabs in popout windows, each with its own Workspace. Its open function opens a window for a model (e.g. from a button in a tabset's toolbar that pops out the tabset), and its render function renders a Workspace into each window. Give the popouts' Workspaces the same dragGroup as the main one so tabs can be dragged between windows: The page's stylesheets are copied into each popout window, which starts out blank. When the user closes a popout window, its tabs are moved back to the main workspace (see the onClose option). A popout window is closed once its last tab is dragged out of it. Popout windows are closed along with the page that opened them (or the component that uses the hook), since it renders their content. Use the "Open in new window" button in a tabset's toolbar below to move the tabset to a new window, then drag tabs between this window and the popout windows. Reset layout Browsers block popup windows that aren't opened in response to user input (e.g. a click), and window.open returns null when that happens; open returns false then, so the tab can be kept where it was.
title: Popout windows

headings.title: Restoring models saved by older versions of an app
headings.text: Restoring models saved by older versions of an app A saved model may refer to tabs that the app no longer has (e.g. a tab that was renamed or removed), or have stale copies of tabs that still exist (e.g. an old title). The normalizeWorkspaceModel function checks a saved model and tidies it the same way the workspace does (e.g. removing tabsets left empty, and fixing the selected tab). Its mapTab option can replace each saved tab with the app's current version, or remove it by returning null: It returns null if the saved value isn't a model, so the app can fall back to its own default model (rather than an empty workspace). The result can also be checked for anything the app requires (e.g. a tab that should always be open) before it's used.

text: A workspace's model is serializable, so it can be saved and restored. Save it from the onModelChanged callback, and restore it with the defaultModel prop: Rearrange the workspace below, then reload the page to see the model restored. Reset layout onModelChanged is called after each change: when a tab is moved, selected, added, or closed, when a tabset is maximized or restored, and when a resize ends (not while the pointer is still moving). Its second argument describes the change. Saved models include each tab's data, so it should be serializable. Models include a version, so that models saved by older versions of the library can be migrated. A malformed model (e.g. one that was saved incorrectly) is replaced with an empty workspace, rather than throwing; in development, a warning is logged. To fall back to a different model instead, check the model with normalizeWorkspaceModel (see below). To restore a saved model after the workspace has mounted (e.g. a "reset layout" button), use the imperative setModel method. Content that isn't part of the model (e.g. the text in a notes tab) isn't saved; tabs can save it in their data with the updateTab method. The example above works well with client-rendered applications. For server-rendered applications, see server rendering.
title: Persistent layouts

text: By default, users can close and drag any tab, and drop it anywhere. Restrictions are opt-in: A tab's disableClose and disableDrag flags prevent the user from closing or dragging it. Other tabs can still be dropped around it. A tabset's disableDrag flag prevents the user from dragging the whole tabset (its tabs can still be dragged). Tabsets that contain a tab with the disableDrag flag can't be dragged either. The disableDrop prop rejects drop targets: either all of them, or the ones a function returns true for. While a tabset is dragged, the function is called for each of its tabs, so a tabset can only be dropped where all of its tabs could be. Tabs dragged in from outside of the workspace (see dragging tabs in) use source: "new". The disabled prop locks the arrangement: tabs can't be resized, dragged, dropped, or closed (but they can still be selected, and tabsets maximized). For example, a tab can opt out of being closed or dragged, and a tabset's data can be used to decide whether it accepts drops: Drops at the edges of the workspace (beside all of the tabsets) don't have a tabsetId, so the function checks for an edge before looking up the target tabset. None of these restrict the imperative API; it can still be used to add, remove, or re-arrange tabs. The exception is startExternalDrag , which starts a user drag and is checked like one. In the workspace below, the "Pinned" tab can't be closed or dragged, and other tabs can't be dropped into its tabset. Lock workspace (disabled) Prevent closing tabs (disableClose)
title: Restrictions

headings.title: Keyboard and accessibility
headings.text: Keyboard and accessibility Tabsets follow the ARIA tabs pattern: each tab list has role="tablist", each tab has role="tab", and each tab's content has role="tabpanel", linked to its tab. Only one tab per list (normally the selected one) is in the page's tab order; within a list, focus moves with the arrow keys: ← and → (or ↑ and ↓ when tabs are placed on the left or right) move focus to the previous or next tab, wrapping at the ends Home and End move focus to the first or last tab Enter or Space selects the focused tab Delete or Backspace closes the focused tab (unless closing is disabled) and moves focus to its neighbor Tabs use manual activation: moving focus doesn't select a tab, so arrowing past a tab doesn't mount its content. Separators between tabsets can be resized with the keyboard like any other Separator .

text: By default, a workspace renders an unstyled Separator between tabsets. It takes up no space and can't be seen, so tabsets are resized by dragging the boundary between them (like in the basics demo). Rendering visible separators with the renderSeparator prop is recommended; it receives the orientation of the split, so separators between tabsets side by side can be given a width and those between stacked tabsets a height: Reset layout Visible separators show users where tabsets can be resized, and give them something to grab. Separators are tab-focusable window splitters, so tabsets can be resized with the keyboard (by the default separators too); a visible separator can also show keyboard users which one has focus. To render no separators at all, return null from renderSeparator. Tabsets can still be resized by dragging the edges between them, but not with the keyboard.
title: Separators and accessibility

headings.title: Tab content
headings.text: Tab content Workspaces render their tabsets and tabs on the server. Tab content isn't server rendered by default, though: it's rendered through portals (so that moving a tab doesn't remount it), which React can't render on the server. Instead, it's rendered once hydration has finished. The serverRenderTabContent prop renders the content of selected tabs on the server. It can be true, or a function to choose per tab: Server-rendered content is rendered inline (within its tabset's tab panels) on the server and while hydrating, then moved into a portal. Moving the content into a portal remounts it once (e.g. resetting its state and re-running its effects), so this is best suited to content that is cheap to mount and benefits from being in the server-rendered HTML. This prop has no effect for workspaces that aren't server rendered.

headings.title: Saved models
headings.text: Saved models A saved model has to be available on the server too, so that the server and client render the same model. Saving it in localStorage doesn't work, since the server can't read it; a cookie (or other storage the server can read) does: Don't read localStorage while rendering (e.g. only when window is defined): the client would render a different model than the server, causing hydration errors. Cookies are limited to about 4KB, which a workspace with many tabs (or a lot of tab data) can exceed. Larger models can be saved on the server (e.g. with the user's settings) and passed in the same way.

text: Like the rest of the library, workspaces are unstyled. The classNames and styles props apply class names and inline styles to the elements a workspace renders: Tabsets re-render when these objects (or the render props) change, so in large workspaces define them outside of the component (or memoize them) rather than inline. Entries for the elements of a tabset, tab, or split can also be functions of it (and its state, like useParentTabsetState returns), e.g. to style tabsets and tabs by their data: Each element also has a data attribute (e.g. data-tab), and exposes its state as data attributes, which can be used for styling: Elements within a tabset have a data-tab-placement attribute (see tab placement). Each split is a Group with data-split and data-split-id attributes; its gap (set with the split entry of classNames or styles) adds space between tabsets, and counts toward their minimum sizes. Separators between tabsets are rendered by the renderSeparator prop, which should return a Separator (or null, in which case tabsets can still be resized by dragging their edges). Elements within a collapsed tabset have a data-tabset-collapsed attribute, and their data-tab-placement is the side its header runs along while collapsed (e.g. "left" for a sidebar). The content of the element that follows the pointer while a tab is dragged can be customized with the renderDragPreview prop (and while a tabset is dragged, with the renderTabsetDragPreview prop). A tabset being dragged has a data-tabset-dragging attribute. Event handlers for tabsets (e.g. a context menu for tabset headers) can be attached to the Workspace itself, and find the tabset from the event's target: A maximized tabset is rendered above the rest of the workspace, so it should have a background.
title: Styling

text: Components within a tab can use the useParentTab hook to close or select the tab, and useParentTabState to re-render when it's selected or shown. The useParentTabset and useParentTabsetState hooks do the same for the tabset, and useParentWorkspace returns the workspace's imperative API. By default, the content of tabs that aren't selected stays mounted. The hiddenTabBehavior prop can unmount it instead (e.g. for memory-intensive content), or render it within a hidden React Activity so that its effects are unmounted. With "mount-on-show", content isn't mounted until its tab is first visible (selected, in a tabset that isn't collapsed or covered by a maximized tabset; floating tabsets are never covered), and then stays mounted (e.g. for expensive content in tabsets with many tabs, or in tabsets that start collapsed). It can also be a function, to choose per tab. Activity requires React 19.2 or newer; with older versions, "activity" behaves like "keep-mounted". Moving a tab preserves its content's React state, but its elements are moved within the document, which resets some browser state: iframes are reloaded, playing media is paused, and focused elements are blurred. Tabs are rendered using portals so that moving a tab won't cause a remount. Because of this, tab content is not server rendered by default. See server rendering to opt into server rendering.
title: Tab content

headings.title: Mixing placements
headings.text: Mixing placements Tabsets can override the workspace's placement with the tabPlacement field of their model node: Tabsets created by dragging a tab to the edge of another tabset use the workspace's tabPlacement prop.

text: Tabs can be placed on any side of a tabset with the tabPlacement prop: Tabs placed on the left or right are stacked: dropped tabs are inserted based on their vertical position, and the up and down arrow keys move between tabs. top bottom left right Elements within a tabset have a data-tab-placement attribute, which can be used to style them for each placement (see styling). The left and right placements are the start and end of a tabset, so in a right-to-left layout (e.g. within dir="rtl") tabs placed on the left are on the right. Styles for them should use logical properties (e.g. border-inline-end rather than border-right), like the demo above does. Tabs on the left or right don't have to be rotated; the demo above rotates them with the writing-mode CSS property, but a vertical list of unrotated tabs works too.
title: Tab placement

Ignore layout changes resulting from imperative API calls or window resize events. storage ?: LayoutStorage = localStorage Storage API; responsible for reading and writing saved layouts.

text: The useDefaultGridLayout hook saves and restores grid layouts (both columns and rows) between page loads. It can be configured to store values using localStorage, sessionStorage, cookies, or any other persistence layer that makes sense for your application. It works the same way as the useDefaultLayout hook does for groups; refer to the persistent layouts section for more examples of how to best use it in your client or server-rendered application. A saved layout is ignored for an axis if its track ids don't match the Grid's (e.g. after a column has been added or removed).
title: useDefaultGridLayout

headings.text: Parameters debounceSaveMs ?: number = 100 Debounce save operation by the specified number of milliseconds; defaults to 100ms This parameter corresponds to the deprecated onLayoutChange callback. Code using the new onLayoutChanged callback (shown above) does not need to be debounced. id : string Uniquely identifies a specific group/layout. onlySaveAfterUserInteractions ?: boolean Only auto-save layouts that were directly caused by user input (e.g. keyboard or mouse events). This prevents layout shift for server-rendered apps. It can be configured to store values using localStorage, sessionStorage, cookies, or any other persistence layer that makes sense for your application. Refer to the persistent layouts section for more examples of how to best use the hook in your client or server-rendered application.

For example, a button rendered within a Cell can resize one of the Grid's columns: Returns null if the component isn't rendered within a Grid. The returned value doesn't change when the Grid's layout changes, so this hook doesn't cause components to re-render.

The returned value doesn't change when the Panel is resized, so this hook doesn't cause components to re-render.

Use useParentTabState for values that should trigger a re-render.

For example, an editor can close its tab when its file is deleted: Returns null if the component isn't rendered within a tab. The returned value doesn't change for the life of the tab (even when it's moved), so it's safe to use as an effect dependency.  This is true even if the tabset is covered by another, maximized tabset.

 While a separator is being dragged, this reflects how the tab's tabset is shown (e.g. collapsed as soon as it reaches its collapsed size),
which the model only reflects once the drag ends; it also reflects tabsets that are collapsed to fit (see TabsetNode.collapsible).

text: The useParentTabState hook returns the state of the nearest tab. Components that use it re-render when that state changes. For example, an editor can focus itself whenever its tab is shown: Returns null if the component isn't rendered within a tab. A tab can be selected but not visible, if its tabset is covered by another, maximized tabset. Use isVisible to pause work while a tab can't be seen, and useParentTab to control the tab.

and when it's collapsed to fit (see TabsetNode.collapsible); useParentTabsetState().isCollapsed reflects how it's shown.

text: The useParentTabset hook returns the nearest tabset. Components rendered within a tabset (e.g. by the Workspace's renderTabsetToolbar prop) or within the content of one of its tabs can use it to add tabs to it or to maximize it. For example, a button in a tabset's toolbar can add a new tab to that tabset: Returns null if the component isn't rendered within a tabset. The returned value doesn't change for the life of the tabset, so it's safe to use as an effect dependency. Use useParentTabsetState for values that should cause components to re-render.
title: useParentTabset

headings.title: Return value
headings.text: Return value useParentTabsetState : () => ParentTabsetState | null See ParentTabsetState (below).

headings.title: ParentTabsetState
headings.text:
ParentTabsetState State of the nearest ancestor tabset (returned by useParentTabsetState).
 isActive : boolean The user most recently interacted with this tabset (by pointer or focus).
 isCollapsed : boolean The tabset is collapsed to just its header.
 While a separator is being dragged, this reflects how the tabset is shown (e.g. collapsed as soon as it reaches its collapsed size),
which the model (and useParentTabset().isCollapsed()) only reflects once the drag ends.
 A tabset that's collapsed to fit (see isCollapsedToFit) is collapsed, although the model has it expanded.
 A maximized tabset is shown expanded, but it's still collapsed when it is restored.
 isCollapsedToFit : boolean The tabset is collapsed only because it doesn't fit (e.g. the workspace is narrower than its tabsets' minimum sizes; see TabsetNode.collapsible).
The model has it expanded, and it's shown expanded again once it fits.
 It can't be expanded until then (e.g. useParentTabset().expand() does nothing), so a toolbar can hide (or disable) its "expand" button.
 isCollapsible : boolean The tabset can be collapsed (or is collapsed, and can be expanded), e.g. to show or hide a toolbar button:
it has the collapsible flag, isn't the only tabset in the workspace, and has a sibling that isn't collapsed (or it's floating; see FloatingTabsetNode).
 isDragDisabled : boolean The user cannot drag the tabset as a whole, because:

It has the disableDrag flag, or one of its tabs does
The Workspace has the disabled prop
It's the only tabset in the workspace (see isRoot), and can't be dragged to another workspace (see the Workspace's dragGroup prop; tabsets with the keepWhenEmpty flag can't be)
A tabset is maximized

 Dragging a floating tabset moves it (rather than dropping it elsewhere), so only its own disableDrag flag and the Workspace's disabled prop prevent that;
they also prevent it from being resized.
 isFloating : boolean The tabset floats above the layout (see WorkspaceModel.floating).
 isMaximized : boolean The tabset is maximized.
 isRoot : boolean The tabset is the root of the model, so it's the only tabset in the workspace.
 Some controls aren't useful for the only tabset (e.g. maximizing it), so this can be used to hide them.
 selectedTabId : string | undefined Id of the selected tab.

text: The useParentTabsetState hook returns the state of the nearest tabset. Components that use it re-render when that state changes. For example, a button can show whether its tabset is maximized: Returns null if the component isn't rendered within a tabset. Use useParentTabset to control the tabset.
title: useParentTabsetState

headings.title: Return value
headings.text: Return value useParentWorkspace : () => ParentWorkspace | null See ParentWorkspace (below).

headings.title: ParentWorkspace
headings.text:
ParentWorkspace The nearest ancestor Workspace (returned by useParentWorkspace), including its imperative API.
 It includes every method of the WorkspaceImperativeHandle (the imperative API), along with these values: id : string Id of the Workspace.

text: The useParentWorkspace hook returns the nearest Workspace, including its imperative API. Components rendered within a Workspace (including tab content) can use it to open, close, and arrange tabs without passing refs or props down to them. For example, a link within a tab can open a file in another tab. addTab adds it to the active tabset (the one the user most recently interacted with), or selects its tab if it's already open: Returns null if the component isn't rendered within a Workspace. The returned value doesn't change when the Workspace's model changes, so this hook doesn't cause components to re-render.
title: useParentWorkspace

headings.title: Customizing popout windows
headings.text: Customizing popout windows The onOpen option is called with each new window and the element its content is rendered into, before the content is rendered: Stylesheets are copied as they are when the window opens, including rules that CSS-in-JS libraries insert with insertRule, and stylesheets added to the page's head afterward are copied too. Rules inserted into an existing stylesheet afterward aren't; libraries that insert rules as components render can usually be configured (e.g. in onOpen) to insert them into the new window's document instead. Setting copyStyles to false stops all copying, including the page's plain stylesheets, so it's usually best left on. Stylesheets removed or edited in place after they're copied aren't updated in popout windows.

headings.title: Saving and restoring popout windows
headings.text: Saving and restoring popout windows The onCloseAll option is called with each popout window's model and position when the page is closed (or reloaded) or the component that uses the hook unmounts (e.g. a route change), just before the popout windows are closed (this includes when the component is hidden by Activity, and Fast Refresh in development). Browsers won't open them again until the user interacts with the page, so restore them from a click. Windows that the browser blocks (open returns false) are kept so they can be reopened later (but are lost if the page is closed again first, since onCloseAll replaces the saved state). The main workspace's model must be saved too (see persistence), or restored popouts will duplicate tabs it shows again. Calling open with a model that has no tabs does nothing: Some browsers only open one popup window per click.

headings.title: Options
headings.text: Options usePopoutWindows : (options: UsePopoutWindowsOptions) => PopoutWindows See UsePopoutWindowsOptions and PopoutWindows (below).

headings.title: UsePopoutWindowsOptions
headings.text:
UsePopoutWindowsOptions Options for usePopoutWindows.
 copyStyles ?: boolean | undefined Copy the page's stylesheets into each popout window when it's opened (and stylesheets added to the page's head afterward).
Defaults to true; if false, none of the page's styles (including plain stylesheets) are copied.
 The rules of <style> elements are copied (including rules inserted with CSSStyleSheet.insertRule, e.g. by CSS-in-JS libraries)
as they are when the window opens; rules inserted into them later (and stylesheets edited or removed afterward) aren't.
Libraries that insert rules as components render (e.g. Emotion) can usually be configured to insert them into the popup's document instead.
 onCloseAll ?: | ((state: PopoutWindowState<TabData, TabsetData>[]) => void) | undefined Called with each popout window's model and position when the page that opened them is closed (or reloaded),
or the component that uses the hook unmounts, just before the popout windows are closed;
e.g. to save them (and open them again later with open).
It isn't called if there are no popout windows.
 onClose ?: | "discard" | "dock" | ((model: WorkspaceModel<TabData, TabsetData>) => void) | undefined What happens to the tabs in a popout window when the user closes it:

 "dock" (the default) adds them back to the main workspace (see workspaceRef)
 "discard" closes them
A function is called with the popout's model instead (e.g. to save its tabs)

 When docking, a tab is skipped (with a development warning) if the main workspace already has a tab with the same id (its data is not updated, and it isn't selected),
and only the selected tab of the popout's first tabset (that has one) is selected.
 It isn't called when the popout closes because its last tab was moved out of it, or when it's closed by closeAll
(or because the page that opened it is closed, or the component that uses this hook unmounts; see onCloseAll).
 onOpen ?: ((popout: PopoutWindow) => void) | undefined Called when a popout window is opened, before its content is rendered, e.g. to set its title or style its container.
 workspaceRef : RefObject<WorkspaceImperativeHandle<TabData, TabsetData> | null> The main workspace, which tabs are added back to when a popout window is closed (see onClose).

headings.title: PopoutWindows
headings.text:
PopoutWindows Returned by usePopoutWindows.
 closeAll : () => void Close every popout window (without moving their tabs back to the main workspace).
 getState : () => PopoutWindowState<TabData, TabsetData>[] Each popout window's current model and where it is on screen, e.g. to save them (and open them again later with open).
 A popup that reports the opener's exact position as its own (e.g. in Brave) is reported where it was opened instead.
 open : (model: WorkspaceModelInput<TabData, TabsetData>, rect: PopoutWindowRect) => boolean Open a popout window showing a model (e.g. from a button that pops out a tab, or to restore a saved popout).
 Browsers block popup windows that aren't opened in response to user input (e.g. a click),
and some block all but the first one opened for each input.
 Returns: true if the window was opened, or false if it was blocked (or the model has no tabs, in which case no window is opened)
 popouts : PopoutWindow[] The open popout windows.
 render : (renderWorkspace: (props: PopoutWorkspaceProps<TabData, TabsetData>, popout: PopoutWindow) => ReactNode) => ReactNode Render the popout windows' content (each into its window's container, with a portal); render the result alongside the main Workspace.
 
 renderWorkspace Renders a popout's Workspace; spread the given props onto it (along with the same dragGroup as the main Workspace, to drag tabs between windows)

headings.title: PopoutWindow
headings.text:
PopoutWindow A popout window opened by usePopoutWindows.
 container : HTMLElement The element (created by the popup's document, within its body) that the popout's content is rendered into.
 id : string Unique id of the popout (e.g. a React key).
 window : Window The popup window.

headings.title: PopoutWindowRect
headings.text:
PopoutWindowRect Where a popout window is on screen (in screen coordinates) and how big its content is (in pixels); see usePopoutWindows.
 height : number Height of the window's content, in pixels
 screenX : number Horizontal position of the window on the screen
 screenY : number Vertical position of the window on the screen
 width : number Width of the window's content, in pixels

headings.title: PopoutWindowState
headings.text:
PopoutWindowState A popout window's model and where it is on screen, e.g. to save the popouts and open them again later (see usePopoutWindows).
 model : WorkspaceModel<TabData, TabsetData> The popout's current model
 rect : PopoutWindowRect Where the popout is on screen, and its size

headings.title: PopoutWorkspaceProps
headings.text:
PopoutWorkspaceProps Props for the Workspace rendered into a popout window (see PopoutWindows.render).
 The popout window is closed once its workspace has no tabs left (e.g. its last tab is dragged back to the main window);
if the Workspace needs its own onModelChanged prop, call this one from it.
 defaultModel : WorkspaceModel<TabData, TabsetData> The popout's initial model
 onModelChanged : (model: WorkspaceModel<TabData, TabsetData>, meta: WorkspaceChangedMeta) => void Closes the popout window once its workspace has no tabs left
 workspaceRef : RefObject<WorkspaceImperativeHandle<TabData, TabsetData> | null> Used to read the popout's current model (e.g. when it's closed)

text: The usePopoutWindows hook opens tabs in popout windows, each with its own Workspace. Call its open function (e.g. from a button that pops out a tab), and render the Workspaces it returns from render alongside the main one (see popout windows for a demo): The page's stylesheets are copied into each new window. When the user closes a popout window, its tabs are moved back to the main workspace; a popout window is closed once its last tab is dragged out of it, and popout windows are closed along with the page that opened them (or the component that uses the hook). Browsers block popup windows that aren't opened in response to user input, so call open from a click (or another user action). It returns false if the window was blocked.
title: usePopoutWindows

headings.title: Return value
headings.text: Return value useTabListFreeSpace : () => number | undefined The space (in pixels) that the tabs don't use, measured along the tab list (its width, or its height if its tabs are placed on the left or right). It's negative once the tabs overflow, by the amount they overflow. The tab list's --tab-list-free-space custom property has the same value. Each value is measured with the toolbar as it's shown at the time; a toolbar that responds to the free space should do so when it changes (rather than again after the toolbar itself changes, which would count that change twice).

text: The useTabListFreeSpace hook returns the space in the nearest tabset's tab list that its tabs don't use. Components that use it re-render when it changes (e.g. when the tabset is resized, or tabs are added or removed), before the browser paints. For example, a toolbar can move items into a "…" menu once they no longer fit (see custom tabsets for a demo): Returns undefined if the component isn't rendered within a tabset (or the tab list hasn't been measured yet, e.g. while server rendering, or before the component re-renders right after the tabset is first rendered; that re-render happens before the browser paints). To read the free space outside of a tabset (e.g. from a toolbar that's rendered elsewhere and portaled into the tabset), use the getTabListFreeSpace and subscribeToTabListFreeSpace methods of the imperative API.
title: useTabListFreeSpace

headings.title: Parameters
headings.text: Parameters includePartiallyVisible : boolean | undefined Also include tabs that are only partly visible (cut off by an edge of the tab list), e.g. for a menu that lists them too. By default, only tabs that are entirely out of view are included.

headings.title: Return value
headings.text: Return value useTabListOverflow : (options?: { includePartiallyVisible?: boolean }) => string[] Ids of the tabs that are out of view, in the order they're shown. The same array is returned until they change, so it can be used as an effect dependency. Tabs that aren't rendered at all (e.g. hidden with display: none) aren't included.

text: The useTabListOverflow hook returns which of the nearest tabset's tabs are out of view, because its tab list overflows and is scrolled. Components that use it re-render when they change (e.g. when the tab list is scrolled or resized, or tabs are added or removed); apart from scrolling by the user, that happens before the browser paints. For example, a tabset's toolbar can list them in a menu (see custom tabsets for a demo): A tab is scrolled into view whenever it's selected (e.g. with the selectTab method of useParentTabset ), so a menu like this one only needs to select it. No tabs are reported if the component isn't rendered within a tabset (or the tab list hasn't been measured yet, e.g. while server rendering, or before the component re-renders right after the tabset is first rendered; that re-render happens before the browser paints). To read them outside of a tabset, use the getTabListOverflow and subscribeToTabListOverflow methods of the imperative API.
title: useTabListOverflow

text: The useWorkspaceCallbackRef hook returns a ref callback function and value tuple. The value is the imperative Workspace API.
title: useWorkspaceCallbackRef

text: The useWorkspaceRef hook returns a mutable ref object. This hook is useful for situations where you only need a local (to your component) reference to the imperative Workspace API. If you need to share the ref with another component or hook, use the callback ref hook instead.
title: useWorkspaceRef

headings.text: getLayout Get the Grid's current layout: maps of column and row ids to percentages (0..100)

headings.title: getTrackById
headings.text:
getTrackById Imperative API for the column or row with the specified id (see GridTrackImperativeHandle).
 Tracks without an explicit id use their index (e.g. "0") as their id.
 An error will be thrown if the Grid does not contain a matching track.
 
 axis "column" or "row"
 id Track id

headings.title: getTrackByIndex
headings.text:
getTrackByIndex Imperative API for the column or row at the specified index (see GridTrackImperativeHandle).
 The index is resolved to a track id when this method is called; the returned API continues to refer to that id.
Tracks without an explicit id use their index as their id,
so specify ids if the API needs to refer to the same track after tracks are added or removed before it.
 An error will be thrown if the index is out of range.
 
 axis "column" or "row"
 index Track index (starting at 0)

headings.title: setLayout
headings.text:
setLayout Set a new layout for one or both of the Grid's axes.
 
 layout Map of column and/or row ids to percentages (numbers between 0..100)

text:
Imperative Grid API.
 The useGridRef and useGridCallbackRef hooks are exported for convenience in TypeScript projects.
title: GridImperativeHandle

headings.title: collapse
headings.text:
collapse Collapse the track to its collapsedSize.
 This method will do nothing if the track is not collapsible or if it is already collapsed.

headings.title: expand
headings.text:
expand Expand a collapsed track to its most recent size.
 If restoring that size would require collapsing another track, the track expands to the largest size that fits instead (as long as that is at least its minSize).
 This method will do nothing if the track is not currently collapsed.

headings.title: getSize
headings.text: getSize Get the current size of the track in pixels as well as a percentage of its axis (0..100).

headings.title: isCollapsed
headings.text: isCollapsed The track is currently collapsed.

headings.title: resize
headings.text:
resize Update the track's size.
Size can be in the following formats:

Percentage of the axis (0..100)
Pixels
Relative font units (em, rem)
Viewport relative units (vh, vw)

 Numeric values are assumed to be pixels.
Strings without explicit units are assumed to be percentages (0%..100%).
Percentages may also be specified as strings ending with "%" (e.g. "33%")
Pixels may also be specified as strings ending with the unit "px".
Other units should be specified as strings ending with their CSS property units (e.g. 1rem, 50vh)
 
 size New track size

text:
Imperative API for an individual Grid track (column or row); returned by GridImperativeHandle.getTrackById and GridImperativeHandle.getTrackByIndex.
 Sizes are relative to the space available to the track's axis
(e.g. the width of the Grid, minus gaps and gridlines, for a column).
title: GridTrackImperativeHandle

headings.title: setLayout
headings.text:
setLayout Set a new layout for the Group
 
 layout Map of Panel id to percentage (a number between 0..100)

headings.title: collapse
headings.text:
collapse Collapse the Panel to its collapsedSize.
 This method will do nothing if the Panel is not collapsible or if it is already collapsed.

headings.title: expand
headings.text:
expand Expand a collapsed Panel to its most recent size.
 If restoring that size would require collapsing another Panel, the Panel expands to the largest size that fits instead (as long as that is at least its minSize).
 This method will do nothing if the Panel is not currently collapsed.

headings.title: getSize
headings.text: getSize Get the current size of the Panel in pixels as well as a percentage of the parent group (0..100).

headings.title: isCollapsed

resize Update the Panel's size.
Size can be in the following formats:

Percentage of the parent Group (0..100)
Pixels
Relative font units (em, rem)
Viewport relative units (vh, vw)

 Numeric values are assumed to be pixels.

Imperative Panel API
 The usePanelRef and usePanelCallbackRef hooks are exported for convenience in TypeScript projects.
